Every Saturday since she turned thirteen, Wren Delgado had worked the back counter of her father's hardware store, and every Saturday evening she watched him count the small parts. He counted them by weight, as his own father had. Counting two hundred screws by hand took most of an hour; weighing them took a minute. Above each bin he had taped an index card giving the weight of a single piece, and he divided the reading on the scale by that number.

In March the brass hinges began coming up short. The card over their bin said 42 grams, and by the register's records the bin should have held two hundred. The scale said 190. The next Saturday, with the bin restocked to two hundred, it said 186.

Her father moved the hinges behind the counter, where customers had to ask for them, and began keeping an eye on the aisle by the door. He said nothing to Luis, the high school student who unpacked deliveries on Thursdays, but that week Wren found the delivery boxes in the back room slit open and taped shut again. Her father had gone through them a second time after Luis left.

Wren could not make it add up. Who would steal hinges, she wondered, and only hinges, and leave the drawer pulls in the very next bin alone?

She remembered something else instead. In February the store had switched suppliers, after the old one raised its prices, and the hinges from the new company came in green boxes instead of brown. She had unpacked one of those boxes herself. The hinges inside had looked exactly like the old ones.

On Sunday, when the store was closed, she let herself in with the spare key and emptied the bin onto a towel on the counter. She counted the hinges by hand, pushing them into rows of ten. There were two hundred.

Then she sorted them, which took longer. Held edge to edge, the newer hinges had a slightly thinner leaf. She put ten of the new ones on the scale and wrote down the number: 380 grams. Ten of the old ones came to 420.

When her father came down on Monday morning, he found the towel, the rows of hinges, and a new card taped over the bin in her handwriting: OLD 42 g. NEW 38 g. WEIGH SEPARATELY.

He read it twice. Then he picked up the phone and called Luis, and asked whether he could come in on Saturday morning, because there was a job he wanted help with.

That Saturday the three of them went through every bin in the store, weighing ten pieces at a time. The wood screws from the new supplier were off by a fraction of a gram, the washers by less. Her father wrote a fresh card for each bin. On the hinge card, beneath Wren's figures, he added a line of his own: Checked. She was right.

is how to stand with your back to the land
and count. Seven waves, the lifeguard said,
and the seventh is the one that wants you.

the water going back is the part that pulls.

I have watched it take a sandal
from a small boy's foot and carry it out
past the flags, past the line of red buoys,
so fast the boy was still laughing.

early, before the beach fills with towels.

the salt that dries on my arms like chalk.

But I keep the flags where I can see them,
and I count, the way she taught me,
and when the sand begins to move beneath me
I swim along the shore and not against it.

She told us once the sea plays fair.
It shows you everything it means to do,
if you stand with your back to the land,
if you are willing to watch, and count,
and give it the attention it has earned.

My grandmother came to live with us the winter I was eleven. She brought one suitcase of clothes and a second, smaller one that held only thread: spools of every color, a tin of needles, a wooden egg for darning socks, and a pair of scissors shaped like a crane, which she kept for herself.

That February I tore the elbow of my school sweater on the fence behind the gym. It was navy blue, like every other sweater at my school, and I left it on her bed with a note asking her to fix it so that nobody could tell.

It came back two days later with a patch of bright yellow wool woven across the elbow in tiny squares, like the surface of a waffle. You could see it from across the cafeteria. I asked her, as politely as I could manage, whether she had any blue.

She had plenty of blue. She showed me the spool. Then she turned the sweater inside out and showed me the back of the patch, where every thread was knotted and trimmed and the edges of the hole were caught so firmly that the tear was stopped for good. A blue patch, she said, would only pretend the sweater had never been torn, and a pretending repair is the first one to fail.

I wore the sweater because I had to, and for a week I kept my arm bent against my side. Then a girl in my math class asked where I had gotten the yellow, and whether my grandmother would do her backpack.

That spring I looked closely, for the first time, at my grandmother's winter coat. It was covered in small repairs in a dozen colors, green and rust and a violet nearly black, each one neat and plainly visible. When I asked about them, she could name every one: a bus door in the city where she grew up; a nail in a church pew; my mother, aged three, with the kitchen scissors.

The coat was older than my mother. She had never thought of replacing it, she said. A coat with that many stories in it was only getting started.

I am forty now, and my sewing is clumsier than hers ever was. Last month I caught the pocket of my raincoat on a car door and tore it nearly off. My own drawer of thread holds a gray that would have matched exactly. I used the orange.

For forty years the best-selling line of the Garrow Pottery in Tamsford was a set of plates and bowls in a deep, even blue that collectors still call Garrow Blue. The company's catalogs credited the glaze to Edwin Garrow, the founder's son, who told a trade journal in 1891 that it had cost him years of patient experiment.

In 1968, when the old works was being turned into apartments, a carpenter opening a wall in the former mixing room found eleven notebooks wrapped in oilcloth. Each was signed M. Kell. Between 1879 and 1886 their author had recorded more than three hundred glaze trials, numbered in order: the weight of each ingredient, the date, the result, and one thing more, a letter and number giving the shelf in the kiln where the test piece had been fired.

The pottery's wage books identify M. Kell as Martha Kell, a widow with two children, employed as a mixer at a little under half the wage of a kiln man. Nothing else about her has survived.

Trial 312, dated March 1886, matches the recipe for Garrow Blue in the company's formula book, which is written in Edwin Garrow's hand. The match is exact, down to a spelling of cobalt with an extra e at the end, a habit that appears throughout the notebooks and, apart from this one page, nowhere in the company's papers.

What makes the notebooks remarkable, however, is less the final recipe than the method behind it. Cobalt had been used to make blue glazes for centuries, and the glaze men at Garrow knew it well. Their blue came out streaked and uneven. Kell's early trials show the same problem until, around trial 200, she began recording the kiln shelf along with every mixture. Within a few months she had found that an identical recipe fired evenly on the back shelves, where the heat built more slowly, and streaked near the door. From then on she changed one ingredient at a time and fired every test in the same place.

That is the habit of a careful experimenter, and Kell appears to have arrived at it with no training anyone recorded.

Whether Edwin Garrow took her work knowingly is impossible to say. It was common practice for a firm to sell its products under the owner's name, and the formula book may simply have been his record of what the mixing room produced. The catalogs, though, mention only him. A local schoolteacher named Ruth Amsel, who spent six years with the notebooks, put Kell's name on a museum label in 1979, nearly a century after trial 312.

Look closely at an old stone wall, a boulder, or the bark of a tree, and you will probably find patches of gray, green, or orange crust that seem to be part of the surface itself. These are lichens. For most of the history of biology they were classed as single plants, and they remain among the stranger arrangements in the living world.

In 1867 the Swiss botanist Simon Schwendener proposed that a lichen is really two very different organisms living as one: a fungus, and a partner that can make food from sunlight, usually a green alga or a cyanobacterium. Many experts of his day rejected the idea, but later work bore it out. The fungus, which makes up most of the lichen's body, provides the structure. It forms a tough outer layer, anchors the lichen to its surface, and holds on to water. The partner lives in a thin layer just beneath, where light can reach it, and uses photosynthesis to make sugars, much of which passes to the fungus.

Together they can live where neither could easily live alone: on bare rock, on desert soil, on the cold slopes of high mountains, and even in Antarctica. Lichens also tolerate drying out to a degree few plants can match. A dry lichen simply shuts down, sometimes for months, and when it is wetted again it can resume photosynthesis, in some species within minutes to hours.

A lichen has no roots. It takes in water, along with whatever is dissolved in it, directly from rain, fog, and dew. That makes lichens unusually sensitive to air pollution, especially to sulfur dioxide. During the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, many kinds of lichens vanished from the centers of industrial cities, and scientists now survey lichens as a cheap way to check air quality. Where the air has been cleaned up, some of the lost species have returned.

Many lichens also grow very slowly; some crust-forming kinds spread only about a millimeter a year. Geologists have taken advantage of this, using the size of the largest lichen patches on a rock to estimate roughly how long its surface has been exposed, for example since a glacier melted back from it.

Even the basic makeup of lichens is still being worked out. In 2016 a team of researchers reported that many common lichens contain a third partner, a kind of yeast living in the outer layer, which had gone unnoticed for well over a century. A lichen, it turns out, may be less a single organism than a small community. How many members such a community can hold, and what each one contributes, are questions researchers are still trying to answer.
